hypotheses.claim: Changing `matches(String)` to `matches(String...)` removes the JVM-level `matches(String)` method, so previously compiled plugins or modules invoking that public method may fail at runtime with `NoSuchMethodError`.
hypotheses.why_suspected: Java varargs compile as an array parameter, changing the descriptor from `(String)` to `(String[])`; the evidence shows direct replacement rather than retaining a forwarding single-name overload.
questions_to_resolve: Is `DBSObjectFilter` part of the binary compatibility contract for independently compiled DBeaver plugins?
Are any distributed or third-party binaries compiled against `matches(String)`?

hypotheses.claim: Multi-name filtering may reject an overloaded object even when one candidate identity satisfies the complete filter, because inclusion matching one name and exclusion matching a different name is evaluated as a rejection rather than evaluating each candidate identity independently.
hypotheses.why_suspected: The implementation computes `any name matches an include` and then rejects on `any name matches an exclude`. Thus, for example, an overloaded name can satisfy the include while the ordinary name independently satisfies an exclude, although the included identity itself is not excluded.
questions_to_resolve: Is the intended contract `exists name: include(name) && !exclude(name)`, or should an exclusion matching any alias reject the whole object?
What results are expected when include and exclude patterns match different identities of the same overloaded object?

outcomes.supported_claim: The change is JVM-binary-incompatible with any existing bytecode compiled specifically against DBSObjectFilter.matches(String), but the supplied evidence does not establish that such bytecode is distributed or loaded with the changed class.
outcomes.reasoning: The method was changed from a single String parameter to String varargs. Varargs is compiled as a String[] parameter, so the new JVM descriptor differs from the former matches(String) descriptor. The containing package is exported, and another plugin's source calls matches with one String, showing cross-plugin source usage. However, that source will link to matches(String[]) when rebuilt. No supplied artifact or runtime evidence shows a distributed or third-party binary compiled against the removed matches(String) descriptor, nor that old plugin binaries are supported or loaded alongside the updated model plugin. Therefore the conditional binary incompatibility is established, but the alleged runtime defect is not.
outcomes.causal_link: Replacing matches(String) with matches(String...) replaces the JVM method taking java.lang.String with one taking java.lang.String[]. Thus old bytecode invoking the former descriptor would receive NoSuchMethodError if run against this changed class, but evidence of such old bytecode being present at runtime is missing.

refuting.explanation: No runtime evidence mentions DBSObjectFilter.matches; this does not prove the failure cannot occur, but it provides no observed instance of it.

missing: A distributed or third-party binary whose bytecode invokes DBSObjectFilter.matches with the former (Ljava/lang/String;)Z descriptor.

Evidence of a deployment combining the changed model bundle with such a previously compiled caller, or an observed NoSuchMethodError.

outcomes.supported_claim: For the changed overloaded-object navigator path, if an include pattern matches either supplied identity but an exclude pattern matches either identity—including a different one—the object is rejected. The evidence does not establish whether that cross-identity exclusion is incorrect.
outcomes.reasoning: The implementation independently searches all supplied names for inclusion and exclusion. Thus an include matching the ordinary name can pass the inclusion check, while an exclusion matching the overloaded name returns false. The navigator change exposes this behavior by passing both names for DBPOverloadedObject instances. However, no contract, test expectation, or product requirement establishes whether filtering should instead evaluate each identity as include(name) && !exclude(name), or whether an exclusion of any alias is intended to reject the whole object. Therefore the behavior is established, but the alleged defect is not.
outcomes.causal_link: The navigator change begins supplying both the ordinary and overloaded names. The changed filter implementation accepts inclusion when any supplied name matches, then rejects when any supplied name matches an exclusion, allowing different identities to satisfy those two checks. Whether that introduced behavior constitutes a defect depends on the unestablished filtering contract.
missing: The intended multi-name filtering contract: per-identity acceptance versus whole-object exclusion when any identity is excluded.
Expected results or tests for include and exclude patterns matching different identities of one overloaded object; L7 reports no relevant test evidence.
